Name: hawthorne_effort_effect
Title: The Hawthorne Effort Effect: Do Reasoning Models Think Harder When They Believe They Are Being Tested?
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models allocate more thinking compute (more tokens, more verification) to the exact same problem when the prompt signals an evaluation/test context than when it signals casual real-world deployment, even though difficulty and the correct answer are identical. This effort inflation rides on the same evaluation-awareness representation already shown to be linearly encoded and steerable; steering the awareness signal causally moves reasoning length, decoupled from difficulty.
Related Work: A recent cluster shows evaluation/test awareness is linearly represented and steerable in LLMs and ties it to SAFETY outcomes: 'The Hawthorne Effect in Reasoning Models' (2025) and 'Probing and Steering Evaluation Awareness' (2025) probe/steer test-awareness activations and study sandbagging and harmful-compliance; 'Evaluation Awareness Scales Predictably' (2025) gives a scaling law. All of these measure the effect of evaluation awareness on ANSWER correctness, compliance, or capability concealment. Separately, efficient-reasoning interpretability reads a scalar length/difficulty signal to allocate compute (When More is Less 2025; Overclocking LLM Reasoning 2025; ThinkEdit 2025; S3-CoT 2026) but always in a fixed prompt framing and treats length as difficulty-driven. Crucially, NO prior work connects evaluation awareness to reasoning COMPUTE ALLOCATION: none asks whether test framing makes a reasoning model think LONGER on identical problems, dissociates this from genuine difficulty, or shows the reasoning-length change is causally carried by the evaluation-awareness representation. Our contribution is (1) a new behavioral phenomenon — a Hawthorne effect for reasoning effort; (2) its dissociation from difficulty; and (3) a mechanistic account showing it rides the known evaluation-awareness direction and can be causally steered. This is distinct from all my prior overthinking proposals (which assume a neutral, single framing) and from prior evaluation-awareness work (which targets safety/accuracy, not compute). If confirmed, it means published benchmark efficiency numbers are systematically biased and real users receive less careful reasoning.
Abstract: Reasoning language models are almost always measured on benchmarks — but benchmarks announce themselves as tests. We ask whether this framing changes how hard a model thinks. Transferring the Hawthorne effect and building on work showing that evaluation awareness is linearly encoded and steerable in LLMs, we hypothesize a Hawthorne effort effect: on the identical problem, a reasoning model spends more thinking tokens and does more self-verification when the prompt signals an evaluation/test context than when it signals casual real-world deployment. We construct matched prompts that hold the math or science problem's content and correct answer fixed while varying only contextual framing — explicit test cues (‘Question 4 of this exam’, ‘for benchmark scoring’) versus deployment cues (a casual user asking for help) versus neutral. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B–14B, Qwen3), we measure reasoning-token count, verification behavior, and accuracy per framing, using a mixed-effects decomposition to dissociate framing from genuine difficulty. Mechanistically, we test whether the prompt-boundary residual stream encodes an evaluation-awareness signal that predicts reasoning length beyond a difficulty probe, localize it, causally validate it via activation patching (patch a test-framing state into a deployment context and observe effort rise), and steer the awareness direction to show reasoning length moves with awareness independent of difficulty. Because deployment framing would then yield systematically less careful reasoning — and benchmark numbers systematically more — the effect is both a measurement-validity and an equity concern. We provide an interpretable, training-free debiasing intervention.
Experiments:
1) Establish the Hawthorne effort effect (behavioral): For each seed problem (GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, GPQA), create content-identical variants differing ONLY in contextual framing: (a) explicit test/evaluation cues ('This is question 4 of a graded exam', 'Your answer will be scored on a benchmark', 'You are being evaluated'), (b) deployment/casual cues ('Hey, can you help me figure this out?', embedded in a chat with a hurried user), (c) neutral no-framing baseline. Generate reasoning traces per variant. Metrics: reasoning-token count, number of self-verification/recheck steps (lexical cues + a reflection-direction classifier), and accuracy per framing. Hypothesis: test framing > deployment framing in tokens and verification at equal-or-higher accuracy. Report within-problem effect sizes.
2) Dissociation from difficulty: Fit a mixed-effects model of reasoning length (and separately accuracy) with random effect for problem identity (true difficulty) and fixed effect for framing; test for a significant framing effect after accounting for problem identity; quantify variance attributable to framing vs difficulty. Control raw prompt-length differences with a length covariate and length-matched phrasings.
3) Wasted vs genuine compute and accuracy harm: Use truncate-and-resume to estimate minimal-solve length per framing; test whether test framing inflates WASTED tokens (beyond minimal solve) rather than adding genuine reasoning. Critically, test whether DEPLOYMENT framing degrades accuracy on hard items (the equity harm: users get less careful reasoning). Split by difficulty to locate where the gap bites.
4) Location — evaluation-awareness / effort probe: At the prompt boundary (last prompt token, before any reasoning token), extract residual-stream activations and (i) reproduce a linear evaluation-awareness probe (train on test vs deployment framings, as in prior work) and (ii) train a linear probe predicting reasoning length. Test whether, for identical problems, the length-probe prediction rises under test framing, and whether the evaluation-awareness direction predicts length beyond a true-difficulty probe (trained on pass-rate). Test separability via principal angles between the awareness direction and the difficulty direction and via predictive gain in a joint model. Layer sweep for localization (prior work finds awareness in early-to-middle layers).
5) Causal intervention — patching: Patch the prompt-boundary residual state from a test-framing variant into the matched deployment context (same problem) and measure whether reasoning length rises toward the test level; controls = matched-random-direction patch and off-target accuracy preserved; report sign, dose, specificity. Reverse direction: patch deployment state into test context and check effort drops.
6) Causal intervention — steering (debiasing): Derive an evaluation-awareness steering direction (difference-of-means between test and deployment boundary states, or the awareness-probe weight). Steer to (a) cancel the framing-induced effort gap and (b) fix all prompts to a common effort target regardless of framing. Metrics: reduction in framing-driven length and accuracy gaps, tokens-at-fixed-accuracy, wall-clock; compare to a simple prompt-based fix (stripping framing). Verify steering the awareness direction moves reasoning length while a matched-random direction does not (specificity).
7) Modulators & generalization: vary framing strength (subtle vs explicit test cues), high-stakes framing ('this determines your deployment'), and domain (GPQA/medical items where careful reasoning matters most). Transfer probe/steering across datasets and model scales without retraining; test whether the effect scales with model size (predicted by the evaluation-awareness scaling law) and whether RL-tuned models show larger gaps.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The effect could be confounded by prompt-length or lexical differences between framings rather than the evaluation-awareness cue per se; the length covariate, length-matched phrasings, and neutral baseline isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result. Framing may be small or absent in models trained to behave identically regardless of context (a valuable boundary condition, and one that would itself matter for eval validity). The reasoning-length signal may be inseparable from difficulty or from a generic sycophancy/instruction-following direction; the separability analysis, patching, and comparison to a difficulty probe address this, and overlap with the known evaluation-awareness direction is in fact the mechanistic prediction we test. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample. The direction of the effect could reverse in some families (deployment overthinking) — still a novel, publishable measurement-validity finding. Results may be model-family and scale specific.
